name: Feature relationship graph
summary: Features drawn as labelled boxes with edges between them, where the edge carries the claim: either a handoff, meaning the tokens one feature promotes are the tokens the next fires on, or a similarity link between features in dictionaries of different widths. It is the shape the paper uses for claims that live between features rather than inside any one of them.
explanation:
### Why this chart and not another

Both claims this shape carries are about relations *between* features, and neither survives being reported one feature at a time.

The first: some [[feature]]s hand off to each other through the generated text — the tokens one raises are the tokens the next fires on, so the pair cycles ([[finite-state-automata-features]]). The evidence is a coincidence between two lists — one feature's top predicted tokens, another's firing set — which a table makes you match yourself, never showing the chain close. The loop is the claim, and only a drawing shows a loop.

The second: [[feature-splitting]] read across dictionary widths. The paper wants to say refinement is not a tree: a feature at one width can descend from two at the width below ([[splitting-is-not-a-tree]]). A dendrogram forbids that by construction. And there is no specificity number to bar-chart — "more specific" is read off short human descriptions, which therefore have to sit on the page where a reader can check them. Boxes of text, not points.

### How to read it, step by step

There are no axes; position is layout. One exception: the splitting graph's horizontal is an ordered sweep of [[dictionary-learning-run]]s — $512$, $4{,}096$, $16{,}384$ features, same transformer, only width changed ([[expansion-factor]]).

A node is one feature — a direction in the 512-dimensional MLP activation space recovered by the [[sparse-autoencoder]], labelled model / run / index ([[feature-notation]]). What fills the box is the evidence for it: in the automaton figures a strip of [[top-dataset-examples]], orange marking the [[feature-activation]] per token, darker for stronger ([[activation-visualization-sampling]]); in the splitting graph, one sentence of authors' description.

The edges are where readers go wrong. In the automaton figures an arrow is not a weight, a wire, or a [[circuit]]. Its label lists the source feature's largest positive [[logit-weight]] entries — the tokens it pushes hardest into the next-token distribution — and it points at the feature those tokens switch on one step later. The handoff travels through the emitted text; nothing inside the model joins the two. So look first at one arrow label, then at the orange tokens in the box it lands on: the same tokens? Then the arrow is earned. Follow them round and see whether you return to the start. A dashed arrow leaving the diagram marks a predicted token no node accounts for.

In the splitting graph an edge means only that a [[masked-cosine-similarity]] cleared a display threshold: cosine between two features' activations over the tokens where the first fires, again over those where the second fires, keep the larger, draw a line above about $0.4$. Colour marks which coarse feature a branch descends from, nothing else.

### What a bad result would look like

For the automata: arrow labels the target box does not highlight; or no cycle, just a chain dribbling out; or labels of generic high-frequency tokens, making the handoff a fact about token statistics rather than these features. Note what is absent: no intervention. Both ends of every arrow are truncated top-$k$ lists from the feature interface — no ablation, no check that emitting the token raises the target's activation. The tidiness is resolution-dependent too: A/0 has 512 features for 512 neurons, not overcomplete ([[overcompleteness]]), and the paper says wider runs split each node and complicate the system.

For the splitting graph: children as broad as their parent, or drifting off its subject. Or sensitivity to the $0.4$ — drop it far enough and everything links to everything; no threshold sweep is shown. The one corroboration beyond descriptions is downstream: the coarse "the in mathematical prose" feature promotes generic continuations (*the theorem*), its fine descendants topical ones (*the classifier*, *the subgroup*).

### Where it comes back

Fig-58 is the reference case: four A/0 features cycling open bracket, tag name, tag close, newline-and-indent, back to open bracket ([[html-feature-automaton]]). Fig-57 runs the shape twice over Unicode, where a character arrives as a prefix byte plus a suffix byte ([[utf8-multi-token-characters]]): Tamil is a clean two-node cycle; Chinese adds a self-loop, a complete single-token character sitting where a suffix would ([[unicode-token-state-machines]]).

Fig-46 keeps the boxes and changes what an edge means entirely. It pulls the other way too: the automata are legible because A/0 is coarse, and the splitting graph is what happens when you stop being coarse.
